questions.question: Explain why soil must be treated as a non-renewable resource in South Africa, describing what soil is, how it forms, and the scale of the national stakes.
questions.expected_answer: Soil is a living blend, not powdered rock: mineral grains weathered from parent rock, decayed organic matter called humus, water, air and billions of organisms, arranged in horizons — dark humus-charged topsoil, paler subsoil, weathered rock and solid parent material — with nearly all fertility concentrated in the thin topsoil, whose humus banks nutrients and moisture and glues particles into stable crumbs. Formation is desperately slow: a few centimetres of topsoil can take several hundred years of weathering, root growth, decay and organism activity, while a single thunderstorm on bare sloping ground can strip more than that in an afternoon — teaspoon deposits against bucket withdrawals, which makes soil effectively non-renewable on any human timescale. The stakes are national because only about 12 per cent of South Africa's land is arable and scarcely 3 per cent genuinely high-potential — one plate in ten feeding sixty million people — yet the country loses an estimated several hundred million tonnes of topsoil a year down its rivers. The protective mechanism is vegetation, the soil's bodyguard: leaves break raindrop impact, roots bind the crumbs, litter feeds the binding humus — and nearly every cause of erosion works by removing that bodyguard.

questions.question: Classify the causes of soil erosion into physical, human and animal families, including the past and present dimension, and describe the evidence of erosion visible across South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Physical causes are the agents: water erodes through an escalating sequence — splash dislodging particles on bare ground, sheetwash skimming a thin film of topsoil, rills cutting small channels, and gullies or dongas where rills deepen — while wind lifts fine dry soil from bare fields, as the 1930s Dust Bowl showed; steep slopes, violent interior thunderstorms, drought cycles and thin cover make South Africa physically erosion-prone, though physical agents mostly complete what land use begins, since bare ground is usually manufactured. Human causes make the ground bare: overcultivation exhausting humus, ploughing straight down slopes so furrows become drains, deforestation for timber and firewood, mining and construction stripping cover — and, in the past, the apartheid homeland system packing too many people and animals onto the smallest, poorest land, engineering the overuse whose donga scars remain in the former Transkei and Ciskei, while poverty, insecure tenure and population growth keep pressing marginal land today. Animal causes centre on overgrazing, which strips grass faster than it regrows, and trampling, which compacts stock paths so water runs off — the daily route to water often becoming a gully's first channel. Evidence: dongas through the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal's Thukela basin and Limpopo's Sekhukhune district; rivers running brown after storms with topsoil in transit; dams like Hazelmere on the Mdloti silting so badly the wall was raised; plus dust plumes, exposed roots and fence posts perched on pedestals of stripped soil.

questions.question: Describe how soil erosion is prevented and controlled in South Africa, and explain how GIS and remote sensing guide that management, defining the key terms.
questions.expected_answer: Prevention keeps soil covered and anchored: on croplands, contour ploughing lays furrows along the contours so each ridge dams runoff, strip cropping alternates cover bands with row crops, rotation and rest rebuild humus, mulching and stubble blanket fields through the dry season, and windbreaks slow erosive wind; on grazing land, stock numbers are held at the veld's carrying capacity, herds rotate between camps so pastures rest, and watering routes are spread so trampling never concentrates. Control repairs open damage: gabions — wire cages packed with rock — and low check dams across gullies trip floodwater so it drops sediment and the floor gradually rises, raw banks are re-vegetated with grasses and hardy shrubs, and healing land is fenced off; national programmes scale this through LandCare, Working for Water clearing invasive aliens that displace binding groundcover, and Working on Fire protecting the vegetation shield. GIS guides the work: spatially referenced data is information tied to coordinates — a gully head's position, a farm boundary, a tagged rain reading. Remote sensing supplies it, described by spatial resolution — the ground size of one pixel, where ten metres sees a field but not a furrow — and spectral resolution — the wavelength bands recorded, with infrared exposing bare or stressed ground early because healthy vegetation reflects it strongly. Features are stored as points (borehole, gully head), lines (river, contour, fence) and areas or polygons (field, catchment, risk zone); overlaying slope, rainfall, soil and vegetation layers maps concentrated risk and tells the teams where the first gabions belong.
